To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neural response to food reward is related to BMI and is mediated by leptin levels and the metabolic status of the participants.
the neural responsiveness to food reward in the ventral striatal reward system is associated with BMI and that this relation is mediated by impaired metabolic satiety signaling.
“Impaired hormonal satiety signals predict the BMI by influencing neural reward responsiveness in the VS, which in turn is associated with food intake.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why some people become obese and others not.
the question how obesity is linked to impaired reward processing in the brain and how the interaction between the brain and the metabolic system influences this relation.
the question, why do some people gain weight while others don’t?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
impaired cross-talk between mesolimbic food reward processing and metabolic signaling predicts body mass index.
the present results indicate that the anticipation of reward in the VS is related to BMI, and this relation is mediated by metabolic signaling.
the present results indicate that a heightened reward motivation for food is a risk factor for obesity and is associated with impaired satiety signaling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individuals with higher BMI show increased activity during the anticipation of reward, which is associated with increased leptin levels.
the anticipation of food reward, which is associated with the VS, is impaired in obese individuals and that this impairment can be explained by impaired satiety signaling.
the anticipation of the pleasure from food intake is a crucial factor for the motivation to eat and hence facilitates overconsumption of palatable foods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the anticipation of food-related rewards may be a key mechanism that contributes to obesity.
the VS, a key brain region for reward anticipation and processing, may play a crucial role in the pathogenesis and treatment of obesity.
a reduced responsiveness to the rewarding effects of food is associated with obesity, which is mediated by the metabolic state.
